segments.t: At Gabriel's apartment, Sofia reveals that she had a drink with pop star Julien Dore. Although Gabriel initially questions why Julien bypassed normal agent protocol, he is thrilled to learn that Sofia has a major recording audition. Let's listen to the scene in French first.
J'ai pris un verre avec Julien Doré.
Vraiment? Pourquoi tu ne m'as rien dit?
Je te le dis maintenant, Gabriel.
Comment a-t-il eu ton numéro?
Je le lui ai donné hier soir.
Il aurait dû m'appeler d'abord.
Ou appeler ton agent officiel, Mathias.
C'est toi qui as tout fait.
C'est grâce à toi, mon amour.
Tu as raison. Et alors?
Je fais des essais de voix demain!
C'est une nouvelle fantastique, chérie.
Et en plus, tu as apporté des chocolats!
Let's examine how Sofia and Gabriel discuss the exciting studio audition step by step to learn natural conversational phrasing.
J'ai pris un verre avec Julien Doré.
'I had a drink with Julien Dore.' Literally 'I took a glass', French uses 'take' with food and drinks where English says 'have'.
Vraiment? Pourquoi tu ne m'as rien dit?
'Really? Why didn't you tell me anything?' Pairing the negative marker with 'nothing' ahead of 'said' builds 'didn't tell me anything' in French.
Je te le dis maintenant, Gabriel.
'I am telling you now, Gabriel.' Both 'to you' and 'it' stack up ahead of 'say' in French — word-for-word, 'I to-you it say now'.
Comment a-t-il eu ton numéro?
'How did he get your number?' Slipping a sounded 't' between hyphens keeps two vowels from clashing when 'has' and 'he' flip order in French.
Je le lui ai donné hier soir.
'I gave it to him yesterday evening.' Compare line two: in French, 'it' stands ahead of 'to him' before 'have given', closed neatly by 'yesterday evening'.
Il aurait dû m'appeler d'abord.
'He should have called me first.' Ending with a two-part chunk that literally means 'of approach' gives the everyday expression meaning 'first of all'.
Ou appeler ton agent officiel, Mathias.
'Or call your official agent, Mathias.' Notice 'official' follows 'agent' in French rather than coming ahead of it as in English.
C'est toi qui as tout fait.
'You are the one who did everything.' Framing casual 'you' inside 'it is you who' spotlights Gabriel's effort, while 'everything' sits before 'done'.
C'est grâce à toi, mon amour.
'It is thanks to you, my love.' Unlike 'because of', this warm expression built from 'grace to' always credits someone for good fortune.
Tu as raison. Et alors?
'You are right. And so?' French says 'you have reason' where English says 'you are right', then nudges the story forward with 'and so?'.
Je fais des essais de voix demain!
'I am doing voice tests tomorrow!' Present action paired with 'tomorrow' works naturally in French for a booked plan, literally 'trials of voice'.
C'est une nouvelle fantastique, chérie.
'That is fantastic news, darling.' A single piece of news is countable in French — literally 'a fantastic new' — closed affectionately with 'darling'.
Et en plus, tu as apporté des chocolats!

'And what is more, you brought chocolates!' Opening with 'and in more' gives a handy chunk you'll hear whenever speakers pile one treat onto another. Now let's listen to the whole scene once more from start to finish.
J'ai pris un verre avec Julien Doré.
Vraiment? Pourquoi tu ne m'as rien dit?
Je te le dis maintenant, Gabriel.
Comment a-t-il eu ton numéro?
Je le lui ai donné hier soir.
Il aurait dû m'appeler d'abord.
Ou appeler ton agent officiel, Mathias.
C'est toi qui as tout fait.
C'est grâce à toi, mon amour.
Tu as raison. Et alors?
Je fais des essais de voix demain!
C'est une nouvelle fantastique, chérie.
Et en plus, tu as apporté des chocolats!

Sofia's talent earns her a coveted voice trial with Julien Dore, celebrating a sweet domestic victory with Gabriel. Let's review the vocabulary and everyday conversational idioms from this scene. See you next time!
Bonne soirée!
